abstract: Noise and external disturbances continuously push the limb away from its intended path, but not every deviation compromises the goal of an action. The accuracy constraints of a task define the range of acceptable endpoints and thereby set its precision demands, that is, how much noise must be attenuated for the task to succeed. Whether neural activity during movement preparation reflects these precision demands remains largely unexplored. We recorded electroencephalography (EEG) while healthy human participants (n = 27) prepared reaching movements toward narrow or wide targets at the same location and with the same timing constraints. An instructed delay before the go cue allowed preparatory activity to be isolated, and mechanical perturbations were applied during movement to probe feedback responses. Narrow targets led to more precise movements, with greater endpoint accuracy, lower variability and smaller perturbation-induced deviations. This was achieved without a reduction in movement speed, and involved greater muscle co-activation and larger long-latency responses to perturbations. Before movement onset, beta power (13-30 Hz) was lower for narrow than for wide targets, an effect that emerged late in the delay period and was concentrated over bilateral parieto-occipital electrodes. In contrast, alpha (8-12 Hz) and theta (4-7 Hz) activity did not differ between conditions. These findings demonstrate that preparatory beta activity is sensitive not only to kinematic requirements of the movement but also the precision with which it must be produced.
